claims.text: The creep resistance of FCC/BCC HEA protective coatings is governed primarily by sluggish diffusion of constituent elements.
Reduced dislocation climb and grain-boundary migration lower the rate of progressive plastic deformation during creep.
High configurational entropy and the multi-element lattice of an HEA produce sluggish atomic diffusion.
The multi-element lattice reduces the mobility of dislocations and grain boundaries.
Creep is expected under continuous loading at approximately 0.5–0.7 times the melting temperature.
Under identical sustained-stress and temperature conditions, the HEA coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate than a conventional single-element or low-entropy alloy coating.
Under identical sustained-stress and temperature conditions, the HEA coating will have a longer time to failure than the conventional coating.
The HEA coating's creep rate will be reduced by at least one order of magnitude relative to the conventional coating, depending on composition and test conditions.
The proposed creep-resistance effect will persist under sustained stress up to 0.7 times the HEA melting temperature.
Persistence of the effect requires a stable microstructure without phase transformations or severe grain coarsening.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction varies with HEA composition and microstructural stability.
The controlled comparison should use HEA and conventional coatings with similar thickness and microstructure under identical loading and temperature conditions.
A creep-rate reduction of less than twofold, or failure to obtain a longer time to failure, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The outcome predicts at least a tenfold creep-rate reduction, but the falsification rule only rejects reductions below twofold. A twofold-to-tenfold reduction could fail the stated quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
